questions.question: What is a closure in Go?
questions.title: When would you use Function Signatures in a real project
questions.direct_answer: A function value that captures variables from its enclosing scope. The captured variables stay alive (and writable) after the outer function returns. Closures give function values state.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A function value that captures variables from its enclosing scope. The captured variables stay alive (and writable) after the outer function returns. Closures give function values state.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Executed — the canonical counter:

```go
func makeCounter() func() int {
    count := 0
    return func() int {
        count++     // captures count — from the ENCLOSING scope
        return count
    }
}

counter := makeCounter()
counter()   // 1
counter()   // 2
counter()   // 3 — state persists across calls
```

makeCounter returned, but count didn't die — the inner function CLOSED OVER it. Each call to the closure reads and writes the SAME count variable. That's the definition: a function + the captured environment it references.

What capture means mechanically: Go closures capture by REFERENCE — the inner function holds a pointer to the variable, not a copy of its value at creation. Writes inside the closure are visible outside (if the outer scope still holds a reference) and vice versa. Two closures created from the same scope share the same captured variables.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OUTER[makeCounter] --> V[count = 0]
    OUTER --> INNER[func int: count++]
    INNER -.->|captures by reference| V
    CALL[counter call] --> IN2[count++ → 1]
    CALL2[counter call] --> IN3[count++ → 2]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The classic interview demonstration — shared state:

```go
func makePair() (func() int, func(int)) {
    n := 0
    return func() int { return n }, func(v int) { n = v }
}
get, set := makePair()
set(42)
get()   // 42 — the getter sees the setter's write
```

One variable, two closures — both see the same n. The pattern generalizes: getters/setters, iterators (the closure holds the loop position), memoization (the closure holds the cache).

What closures are NOT: classes (no methods, no inheritance — just a function with captured state); generators (Go's generators are channels or callback-passing — but the ITERATION state a generator would hold, a closure can); or a performance feature (the capture is a pointer indirection — closures in hot loops are measurable).

The everyday uses: callbacks with context (handler closures capturing a request variable), the error-wrapped deferred closures (the defer topic's pattern), and function values generally (every func value in Go that references its scope IS a closure — there's no separate 'closure type').

questions.question: What is the loop-variable capture trap in Go (pre-1.22)?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Function Signatures
questions.direct_answer: Before Go 1.22, the for-loop variable was ONE variable reused across iterations. Closures capturing it all referenced the SAME slot — after the loop, they all saw the LAST value. 1.22 changed the semantics: each iteration gets a FRESH variable.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Before Go 1.22, the for-loop variable was ONE variable reused across iterations. Closures capturing it all referenced the SAME slot — after the loop, they all saw the LAST value. 1.22 changed the semantics: each iteration gets a FRESH variable.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PRE[pre-1.22: ONE i for all iterations] --> CAP[closures all see i=3 at end]
    POST[1.22+: fresh i per iteration] --> CAP2[each closure sees its own i]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Go 1.22 changed the LANGUAGE: each iteration of a for-loop gets a fresh instance of the loop variable. The closures now capture different variables and return 0, 1, 2 (executed above). The change was safe because the old behavior was almost never intended — the bug dominated any legitimate use.

The interview framing: state the version. 'Since 1.22, each iteration gets a fresh variable — the capture bug is gone' is current truth; 'closures capturing the loop variable see the final value' is the historical truth that explains why millions of lines of Go have i := i in them and why linters still recognize the pattern. Both halves are knowledge; the version boundary is where they meet.
